title: The Return Of Avery Jessup

jokes.text: I'm sorry I taste like Korean cigarettes. Tobacco's the only thing with protein over there. Their meat is just deflated kickballs.
jokes.setup: Avery apologizes for tasting like Korean cigarettes after being held hostage in North Korea.
jokes.punchline: She explains cigarettes are the only protein source, and their meat is 'deflated kickballs' — a surreal, bleak image of North Korean poverty.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from the mundane apology to the absurd detail of 'deflated kickballs' as meat is classic 30 Rock — a confident, weird image delivered straight. Good economy and originality. The 'deflated kickballs' image is genuinely funny and specific.

jokes.text: Earlier today, America's credit rating was downgraded to triple fart-minus.
jokes.setup: Avery delivers a fake news broadcast from North Korean state TV parodying American news anchors.
jokes.punchline: 'Triple fart-minus' as a credit rating designation — absurd but pointed satire of North Korean propaganda about American decline.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words ('triple fart-minus') do all the work. The joke captures North Korean propaganda's childish demonization of America in a single absurd rating. Very 30 Rock in its efficiency.

jokes.text: Jack, this is Scott Scottsman. / My ears are all plugged up from the plane. Am I talking too loud?
jokes.setup: Avery introduces Scott Scottsman, a fellow hostage and sports anchor.
jokes.punchline: Scott's immediate non-sequitur about his ears being plugged from the plane, completely oblivious to the social awkwardness of the moment — and asking if he's talking too loud, which he presumably is.
jokes.explanation: Good character establishment joke — Scott is immediately coded as an oblivious, socially unaware sports-anchor type. The plugged ears detail is a funny mundane intrusion into a fraught emotional reunion scene.

jokes.text: And it's me, Johnny Mountain, with the weather on the one and the traffic on the one. You no ask how I do it.
jokes.setup: The North Korean news broadcast intro parodies local American TV news formats.
jokes.punchline: 'Weather on the one AND traffic on the one' — a surreal double booking of the same time slot — followed by the broken English 'You no ask how I do it,' which is both a bizarre non-answer and a perfect deflection.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout gags. The absurdity of scheduling both weather and traffic at the same time slot is a sharp parody of North Korean media dysfunction, and 'You no ask how I do it' is a brilliant non-sequitur that becomes instantly quotable. Tight structure and maximum originality for a throwaway bit.

jokes.text: I was working for KSCT, out of Scottsdale. They sent me to South Korea to do a 'where are they now?' on the pitcher Byung-Hyun Kim. Turns out he's still living in America, and I get kidnapped.
jokes.setup: Scott explains how he ended up as a North Korean hostage.
jokes.punchline: The tragic anticlimax: he went to cover a 'where are they now' story on a baseball player, discovered the subject never left America, and then got kidnapped — the assignment failed in every possible direction.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating structure: each sentence undercuts the last. The specificity of Byung-Hyun Kim (a real, obscure MLB pitcher) adds a layer of absurdist precision. The triple-fail — wrong country, subject still in America, got kidnapped anyway — is a clean comedy of errors in three beats.

jokes.text: Reminding all of you there is no weekend.
jokes.setup: Scott signs off from the North Korean news broadcast in standard anchor fashion.
jokes.punchline: Instead of a cheerful sign-off, he delivers the bleak North Korean propaganda reminder that there is no weekend — with full anchor gravitas.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first truly excellent joke. Maximum economy — six words that perfectly encapsulate North Korean authoritarian bleakness delivered in the breezy cadence of a local news sign-off. The contrast between the cheerful anchor register and the totalitarian content is perfectly timed. Highly quotable. Comparable to the '8.0 anchor' example in its precision and wit.

jokes.text: If it's a nursery, then you can hear the baby. Or the plant. It's your body.
jokes.setup: Criss suggests an intercom for the upstairs renovation — 'if it's an office you can call down, if it's a nursery you can hear the baby.'
jokes.punchline: 'Or the plant. It's your body.' — pivoting from baby to plant as a delicate euphemism for Liz's ambivalence about having children.
jokes.explanation: Clever use of 'plant' as a running euphemism for baby — immediately establishes the episode's Liz/Criss subplot language. 'It's your body' is a sweet, slightly awkward Criss moment that's both funny and characterful.

jokes.text: At my age, we might have to get an Asian plant or accept an older plant with some behavioral issues, and we're a little afraid of it.
jokes.setup: Liz continues the 'plant' euphemism for having/adopting a child.
jokes.punchline: Translating real anxieties about adoption (age, international adoption, older children with issues) into the plant metaphor creates layered absurdity — especially 'we're a little afraid of it.'
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the plant metaphor to cover adoption anxieties is well-constructed. 'We're a little afraid of it' is the best beat — perfectly captures Liz's neurotic honesty. Strong character integration; only Liz would say this.

jokes.text: Well, I could dip into my 401K... Is something I've heard old people say in commercials.
jokes.setup: Liz considers how to fund the renovation.
jokes.punchline: She starts to say 'I could dip into my 401K' — then reveals she only knows that phrase from commercials, implying she has no retirement savings.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structure — sets up a normal adult statement and then pulls the rug to reveal Liz's financial immaturity. The specificity of 'old people in commercials' is sharp. Very character-specific to Liz's chaotic adulting. Clean, economical, and genuinely funny.

jokes.text: Well, I could chip in. If you take my profits from the hot dog truck and add 'em to the $300 my aunt gave me for Christmas, I'd have $200.
jokes.setup: Criss offers to chip in on the renovation costs.
jokes.punchline: His math is backwards — taking profits plus $300 Christmas money somehow yields only $200, revealing he's losing money on his hot dog venture.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed arithmetic joke — the listener does the math a beat after Criss delivers it, and the realization that his 'profits' are negative is a delayed punchline. The casualness of delivery makes it land harder. Highly quotable and economical. One of the sharper jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Boy, I sound just like my dad. Which, I guess, makes me Mrs. Lemon.
jokes.setup: Criss says 'I gotta get to work,' noting he sounds like his dad.
jokes.punchline: Since Liz is 'Lemon,' if he's her dad, that makes him 'Mrs. Lemon' — a gender-flipped surname gag that also touches on the breadwinner theme.
jokes.explanation: A light, pleasant wordplay gag that also seeds the gender-role reversal theme. Not exceptional but clean and economical.

jokes.text: Tracy, who sponsored your wedding? I don't know. There was a lot of Fanta there, and the police, so maybe they co-sponsored it?
jokes.setup: Jenna asks Tracy who sponsored his wedding, establishing that celebrity weddings have sponsors.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's confusion — he thinks Fanta and the police 'co-sponsored' his wedding because both were present, revealing how chaotic his wedding was.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tracy character comedy — the logic of 'they were there, so they co-sponsored' is perfectly Tracy Jordan: confused, chaotic, but delivered with complete conviction. The Fanta + police pairing implies a beautifully disastrous wedding without spelling it out.

jokes.text: Ms. Maroney, a wedding is a simple and beautiful ceremony where an old man and a crying girl get pushed into the coupling shed.
jokes.setup: Jenna explains that having a sponsor makes you somebody; Tracy responds with his definition of a wedding.
jokes.punchline: 'Pushed into the coupling shed' — Tracy's tribal/archaic definition of marriage as a coercive agricultural ritual, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Tracy Jordan character comedy. 'The coupling shed' is a brilliantly original image — archaic, agricultural, slightly ominous — that could only come from Tracy's uniquely distorted worldview. The structure (simple and beautiful... pushed into the coupling shed) builds perfectly. Justifies the 8+ score: it's imaginative, character-specific, and quotable in a way that only works because we know Tracy.

jokes.text: My sponsor is the Southern Tourism Bureau. It's perfect 'cause I'm sort of a down-home, America's sweetheart type. Leonardi, my hair psychic, is always saying how down to Earth I am.
jokes.setup: Jenna announces her wedding sponsor while describing herself as down-to-earth.
jokes.punchline: The complete lack of self-awareness — she calls herself 'down-to-earth' while naming her 'hair psychic' as a character reference — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Hair psychic' is a perfectly chosen detail — specific enough to be funny, absurd enough to undercut any claim of normalcy. Good Jenna character work, though the irony is fairly standard for her.

jokes.text: They're paying for me and Paul to get married on an old plantation. Which is great 'cause our wedding was gonna be slavery-themed anyway.
jokes.setup: Jenna describes her sponsored plantation wedding.
jokes.punchline: Her 'great cause our wedding was gonna be slavery-themed anyway' — delivered with complete oblivious cheerfulness — is a perfectly dark joke about Jenna and Paul's transgressive aesthetic sensibilities.
jokes.explanation: The darkness works because Jenna delivers it with complete sincerity — the joke is her obliviousness, not the content itself. Some may find it edgy but it's consistent with Jenna's established character of transgressive performativity.

jokes.text: 'cause I'm from le flori-dah pahn-hahndle.
jokes.setup: Jenna insists she has a natural Southern accent because of where she's from.
jokes.punchline: Her pronunciation of 'Florida Panhandle' is itself a deeply mangled, over-performed approximation of a Southern accent — undermining her entire claim in real time.
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining pronunciation is the entire joke — Jenna's 'natural' accent is so affected it instantly disproves her point. Works best as a performance gag (Jane Krakowski's delivery is surely doing heavy lifting) but the written form is still clever structural irony.

jokes.text: Before moving here, I done used to talk-n-jaw like this, see? And when I'm at work, I use my white-people voice. You should see how we talk in the Bronx. Raar blarg shmoo-boo wagga!
jokes.setup: The conversation turns to Southern accents and code-switching.
jokes.punchline: Tracy demonstrates code-switching by performing both a fake Southern drawl AND his 'Bronx' voice — which is pure gibberish ('Raar blarg shmoo-boo wagga!') — suggesting his Bronx voice is equally incomprehensible.
jokes.explanation: The 'Raar blarg shmoo-boo wagga' is classic Tracy Jordan absurdism — the joke is that he's performing incomprehensibility with complete confidence. The structure of demonstrating both voices back-to-back is well-paced.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, sir, I have no idea what you're saying. I'm sure it's nothing that I can't fix with a little accent work.
jokes.setup: Tracy delivers his 'Bronx' gibberish voice.
jokes.punchline: Jenna responds to complete nonsense with 'I'm sure it's nothing I can't fix with a little accent work' — treating gibberish as a correctable dialect problem.
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat — Jenna's breezy confidence that she can 'fix' literal gibberish is a nice character moment. The understatement is well-deployed.

jokes.text: I heard her ask her bear who the dye job is.
jokes.setup: Avery notes that their daughter Liddy is wary of her after the long absence.
jokes.punchline: Liddy called Avery 'the dye job' when talking to her stuffed bear — a child's oblivious cruelty that's also a pointed comment on Avery's appearance.
jokes.explanation: Elegant — uses an offscreen child to deliver a cutting insult without breaking Avery's dignity. The indirection through the bear ('asking her bear') adds a layer of childlike innocence that makes it funnier. Very economical.

jokes.text: There is an iPod 3 and a Mitt Romney 4. They worked all the bugs out. He's not killing hobos at night any more.
jokes.setup: Jack reassures Avery that 'not too much has changed' in her absence.
jokes.punchline: Mitt Romney has a version number (Romney 4.0), and a previous bug involved 'killing hobos at night' — treating a presidential candidate as a software product with literal murderous glitches.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's standout joke. Treating Mitt Romney as consumer software with version numbers and a 'hobo-killing bug' is a brilliantly original political satire concept. The structure is perfect: the product line joke sets up a straight beat, then 'not killing hobos at night' lands as a savage, absurd punchline. It's specific, dark, and utterly quotable. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in craft; exceeds it in originality and cultural specificity. Justifies 8.6/9.0.

jokes.text: And tomorrow, I am going to throw you a Thanks-Christmas-Valen-Easter-Ween of July party.
jokes.setup: Jack wants to celebrate all the holidays Avery missed while held captive.
jokes.punchline: The portmanteau 'Thanks-Christmas-Valen-Easter-Ween of July' — cramming Thanksgiving, Christmas, Valentine's Day, Easter, Halloween, and Fourth of July into one frantic word.
jokes.explanation: The compound word is pleasingly elaborate and the 'of July' at the end is the correct structural punchline within the portmanteau. Not the sharpest joke but executed with commitment and decent originality.

jokes.text: Avery offers blanket forgiveness for anything Jack did while she was gone — Jack's awkward long pause before accepting it.
jokes.setup: Avery says 'if anything happened while I was gone between you and someone else... it doesn't matter now. All is forgiven.'
jokes.punchline: The long pause (inferred from [06:04] timestamp gap after [05:55]) in which Jack visibly processes the guilt of multiple transgressions before accepting.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the gap — about nine seconds of screen time between Avery's offer and Jack's 'okay.' A room of savvy viewers will laugh at the implication of what he's done. Perfect use of awkward silence as a device. Rewatch bonus because it gains meaning once you know the full story.

jokes.text: I've been writing a sex column for Cosmo. Cosmo is my 14-year-old neighbor. He doesn't know anything.
jokes.setup: Liz says she needs relationship advice; Jenna says she's been writing a sex column for Cosmo.
jokes.punchline: Cosmo is revealed to be a 14-year-old neighbor boy, not the magazine — and Jenna's been giving him adult sex advice, which he 'doesn't know anything' about.
jokes.explanation: Textbook misdirection with excellent structure — the setup is a perfect fake-out, the reveal is immediate and clean, and the kicker ('he doesn't know anything') adds a third beat. Maximum economy: twelve words deliver a complete joke with two layers. Justifies 8+ score: the structure is nearly flawless and it's a very quotable Jenna moment.

jokes.text: Sex, money, power, fire, choking, being dragged behind a speed boat... It's all the same thing.
jokes.setup: Liz clarifies she needs money advice, not sex advice.
jokes.punchline: Jenna lists an escalating series of things (sex → money → power → fire → choking → speed boat dragging) as all equivalent, revealing her kink-adjacent worldview where everything collapses into the same erotic/power category.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke — the list starts plausibly ('sex, money, power' — classic), then breaks into dangerous/illegal activities ('fire, choking, being dragged behind a speed boat') that reveal Jenna's personality through escalation. The final item is the perfect absurdist endpoint. Very Jenna.

jokes.text: Paul keeps the house nice, and I try to get him pregnant.
jokes.setup: Jenna explains how she and Paul handle gender role reversal as breadwinner and homemaker.
jokes.punchline: 'I try to get him pregnant' — Jenna applying the reversed gender roles to their literal biological limits, with Paul being biologically male.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully compressed absurdist joke — Jenna has taken the gender-reversal premise to its biological extreme with complete sincerity. Perfect economy (six words for the punchline), high quotability, and deeply character-specific. Paul and Jenna's unconventional relationship makes this not random but earned.

jokes.text: If I want to treat myself to a new pair of Christy LaButtons, I don't have to ask any man for $17.
jokes.setup: Jenna celebrates financial independence as a breadwinner.
jokes.punchline: Her luxury indulgence is 'Christy LaButtons' — knockoff shoes — that cost $17. The joke is in the pathetic price point undercutting her feminist triumphalism.
jokes.explanation: The $17 price point is the key detail — it deflates the feminist empowerment speech with mundane reality. Works as setup for the LaButtons/Louboutins reveal in the next beat.

jokes.text: They're knockoff Christian Louboutins. I got tired of ruining $1,200 shoes trying to impregnate my boyfriend.
jokes.setup: Liz asks about 'Christy LaButtons'; Jenna explains they're knockoffs.
jokes.punchline: She specifies why she switched to knockoffs: she kept 'ruining $1,200 shoes trying to impregnate my boyfriend' — a callback to the pregnancy joke that implies vigorous, shoe-destroying activity.
jokes.explanation: This is a callback that's funnier than the original setup. The combination of the knockoff shoe revelation PLUS the absurd reason (ruining Louboutins during pregnancy attempts) is layered, character-specific, and highly quotable. The structure is perfect: straightforward product name question → knockoff explanation → impossible-situation explanation. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Feminism promised us two things... Fatter dolls, and an end to traditional gender roles.
jokes.setup: Liz is convinced by Jenna's argument to embrace being the breadwinner.
jokes.punchline: 'Fatter dolls' as the first promise of feminism — the absurdly mundane and specific reduction of feminist achievement to doll body types.
jokes.explanation: Liz reducing feminism to 'fatter dolls and gender roles' is a sharp, self-aware joke about how feminism gets trivialized — and also a very Liz thing to say. Good character integration, strong economy.

jokes.text: You wear the pants, Liz. You don't necessarily pull them off because of your hips, but you wear them.
jokes.setup: Jenna encourages Liz to embrace being the breadwinner.
jokes.punchline: The backhanded compliment: 'you wear the pants' (empowering) → 'you don't necessarily pull them off because of your hips' (body-shaming pivot) — Jenna's compliments always contain poison.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed backhanded compliment that plays on the double meaning of 'pull them off' (wear successfully vs. remove). The pivot from empowerment to body criticism is very Jenna — she can't help herself. The economy of execution is excellent.

jokes.text: An hour for the year? Am I supposed to just scratch the surface of Channing Tatum's meteoric rise?
jokes.setup: Jack asks Liz to prepare a one-hour pop culture presentation for Avery.
jokes.punchline: Liz is outraged that one hour isn't enough, specifically because it would only allow her to 'scratch the surface' of Channing Tatum's rise — her pop culture obsession is absurdly specific.
jokes.explanation: Good Liz character comedy — her earnestness about pop culture depths is funny. The specificity of Channing Tatum (who had just had his breakthrough year with Magic Mike) adds timeliness.

jokes.text: That woman does not forgive. She's still furious with Al Gore for stealing George Bush's idea to have an Internet.
jokes.setup: Jack finds Avery's blanket forgiveness suspicious and out of character.
jokes.punchline: Jack's evidence that Avery never forgives: she believes Al Gore stole the Internet from George Bush — a precise inversion of political reality that reveals both Avery's and Jack's extreme conservative worldview.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant joke — the inversion of the Al Gore/Internet story is funny on its own, but deployed as a character establishment detail ('she's STILL furious') makes it both a political joke and a character joke simultaneously. The specificity ('stealing George Bush's idea to have an Internet') is perfect. Justifies 8+ — it's doing double duty with great economy.

jokes.text: Soccer, jazz, infidelity.
jokes.setup: Jack asks what people don't want to talk about when they change the subject.
jokes.punchline: Liz's list: 'soccer, jazz, infidelity' — the first two being boring topics and the third being a serious offense, casually grouped together.
jokes.explanation: Three-word list joke with perfect rhythm — the rule of three where item three subverts the pattern. Soccer and jazz are boring; infidelity is not. The deadpan delivery implied by context makes it land. Maximum economy (three words for the punchline). Very quotable.

jokes.text: Okay, first of all, I don't know what you count as cheating, but she was forced to marry someone else. Kim Jong-Un, Lemon. Have you seen news footage of that man? I have so many missile! I even have nuclear missile. Just for you, sugarprong.
jokes.setup: Jack raises red flags about Scott Scottsman and Avery's possible infidelity; Liz points out she was FORCED to marry Kim Jong-Un.
jokes.punchline: Jack impersonates Kim Jong-Un with broken English bragging about missiles and the non-sequitur term of endearment 'sugarprong.'
jokes.explanation: 'Sugarprong' is a magnificent invented term of endearment — bizarre, slightly threatening, entirely original. The broken English missile boasting is a familiar bit but 'sugarprong' elevates it. Very quotable.

jokes.text: You French-Canadian kissed her mother, which is my name for French kissing when it bums everybody else out.
jokes.setup: Liz calls out Jack's hypocrisy for questioning Avery's fidelity.
jokes.punchline: 'French-Canadian kiss' — Liz's invented euphemism for French kissing Avery's mother, defined as 'French kissing when it bums everybody else out.' The neologism is perfect.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'French-Canadian kissing' as a term for disgusting/inappropriate French kissing is brilliantly original wordplay — the Canadian modifier implies something similar but wrong, which is exactly what it means. Liz's self-definition ('which is my name for...') adds a meta-layer. Highly quotable, very original. Justifies 8.4: comparable to the '8.0 anchor' and arguably better in originality.

jokes.text: The game is afoot! / No. She's been back for, like, six hours. Maybe take a little time, let things get back to normal. / Playing psycho-sexual mind games is our normal, Lemon.
jokes.setup: Jack announces he'll use guilt to interrogate Avery.
jokes.punchline: Liz suggests normalcy; Jack counters that psycho-sexual mind games ARE their normal.
jokes.explanation: Good Jack character joke — 'psycho-sexual mind games is our normal' is a precise summary of the Jack/Avery relationship dynamic and delivered with his characteristic pomposity.

jokes.text: Dadgum possum up and what been bit my mother's neck brace.
jokes.setup: Jenna practices her Southern accent for the commercial.
jokes.punchline: The line itself is pure Southern-accent gibberish — grammatically incoherent, a word salad of Southern signifiers ('dadgum,' 'possum') that doesn't mean anything.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Jenna's 'Southern' sentence is complete nonsense assembled from Southern-sounding words — revealing she doesn't understand Southern dialect, she's just pattern-matching. Each repeated attempt that gets worse is a good running escalation.

jokes.text: Again, you waste of my time!
jokes.setup: Jenna struggles to get the accent right; the coach demands she try again.
jokes.punchline: The dialect coach's exasperation breaks professional norms — 'you waste of my time!' is an unusually personal insult that reveals how genuinely frustrated they are.
jokes.explanation: A functional background character reaction joke. Gets the job done but not particularly original — the exasperated coach type is well-worn territory.

jokes.text: Dixie's callin', y'all. I reckon you should answer. / No, this isn't right. This isn't Southern elegance. This is a dirtbag girl I once knew. A girl named Jay-nuh!
jokes.setup: After extensive coaching, Jenna finally nails the commercial line.
jokes.punchline: The director says 'Excellent!' but Jenna rejects the successful take — hearing her true 'Jay-nuh' self in her own voice terrifies her.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Jenna's identity crisis is dramatized by her rejecting the very take the director wants. 'A girl named Jay-nuh' (the Southern pronunciation of Jenna) is a nice touch. Her self-disgust at recognizing herself is relatable and funny.

jokes.text: She used to get into fistfights at water parks, and lost her virginity to a bait salesman on a water bed.
jokes.setup: Jenna describes her former trashy self, Jay-nuh.
jokes.punchline: The specific details — water park fistfights and bait salesman on a water bed — are perfectly calibrated trashy Southern backstory details.
jokes.explanation: The specificity is what elevates this beyond a generic 'she was trashy' joke. 'Bait salesman' is perfect — not a fisherman, not a car salesman, a BAIT salesman. The water bed is exactly right. These details feel lived-in and specific to Jenna's character history.

jokes.text: She's not who I am any more. I'm classy. People who say that about themselves usually are.
jokes.setup: Jenna insists she's classy now and not that person.
jokes.punchline: Liz's deadpan: 'People who say that about themselves usually are' — complete sarcasm delivered as if it's a sincere observation.
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan economy — eight words of pure sarcasm delivered straight. One of Liz's cleanest reaction lines in the episode. The structure is textbook: statement of fact that's actually the opposite.

jokes.text: Kim Jong-Il could not be reached for comment because he was having a totally normal day being alive and not dead.
jokes.setup: Cut to another North Korean broadcast segment.
jokes.punchline: The transparent lie: 'totally normal day being alive and not dead' — the North Korean regime's denial of Kim Jong-Il's death in the most obvious possible way.
jokes.explanation: Excellent political satire joke. 'Totally normal day being alive and not dead' is beautifully absurd denial-language — the very act of specifying 'alive and not dead' confirms the opposite. The deadpan news-anchor delivery amplifies it. Timeliness is strong (Kim Jong-Il had recently died). Justifies 8+

jokes.text: In NBA action, Kim Jong-Un won the championship today. Our brilliant comrade scored 200 points and then went hot-tubbing with a couple guys he's definitely just friends with.
jokes.setup: Scott delivers North Korean sports news.
jokes.punchline: 'Definitely just friends with' — the transparent denial of Kim Jong-Un's rumored homosexuality/relationships in the context of North Korean propaganda, plus scoring 200 points in basketball is absurd propaganda inflation.
jokes.explanation: The 'definitely just friends with' construction is the highlight — the qualifier 'definitely' doing the opposite of what it claims. '200 points' is also a nice escalation of North Korean propaganda absurdity. Paired with joke #42, these broadcast segments form a consistently strong running gag.

jokes.text: Thank you. I forgive you. You lose, Jack... Is what Kim Jong-Il said to Jack Nicklaus after defeating him in golf today because they're both totally alive.
jokes.setup: Jack confesses to having feelings for another woman; Avery forgives him again. Cut to North Korean broadcast.
jokes.punchline: Scott uses Jack's phrase 'you lose' as the segue into the news tag about Kim Jong-Il beating Jack Nicklaus in golf — 'because they're both totally alive.' Callback to both the mind games and the 'totally alive' running joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural callback — 'You lose, Jack' transitions into North Korean propaganda seamlessly, and 'they're both totally alive' builds on the established running joke. The Jack Nicklaus golf detail (referencing North Korean propaganda claims about Kim Jong-Il's golf prowess) is historically specific and funny.

jokes.text: You went out and bought a Fedora. This? I finally watched the premiere of Prime Suspect on Hulu. It's really very good. Anyway, I thought I would treat myself.
jokes.setup: Criss shows up wearing a Fedora after presumably a good day.
jokes.punchline: Criss justifies a Fedora by saying he finally watched a TV premiere on Hulu — a wildly disproportionate self-reward, and the Fedora itself signals his slight hipster pretension.
jokes.explanation: Good Criss character beat — the Fedora as self-reward for watching a Hulu premiere is a specific, slightly sad millennial man moment. Works as character comedy more than a pure joke.

jokes.text: I'm a man. I'm a man, I'm a man! I'm an adult man! You think I like you having to pay for everything? It's humiliating.
jokes.setup: Criss objects to Liz's condescending treatment of his money situation.
jokes.punchline: The repeated escalating declaration 'I'm a man, I'm a man, I'm an adult man!' — the need to specify 'adult' undermines the declaration of masculinity.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'man' to 'adult man' is the tell — he's working too hard to convince himself. Good escalation structure, though not particularly original.

jokes.text: Only because liking the crisspoints system is one of the ways I earn crisspoints!
jokes.setup: Liz questions whether he liked the crisspoints system.
jokes.punchline: He reveals that expressing satisfaction with the system is itself a way to earn points within the system — a beautifully circular, self-defeating logic.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. The logical structure is perfect: if you earn crisspoints by liking the crisspoints system, you can never authentically express approval of it. It's a recursive trap — a domestic Catch-22. The structure is flawless, the economy is maximum, and it deepens the original crisspoints joke enormously. This is comparable to the 9.5 anchor example in structural elegance. The best joke in the episode justifying the highest score.

jokes.text: You're the one who chose to sell hot dogs out of a car. / It is a van with a car engine, Liz, okay?
jokes.setup: Liz criticizes Criss's business.
jokes.punchline: Criss's defensive distinction: it's a 'van with a car engine' — a classification that implies it's somehow better than a car, but the distinction is meaningless and slightly sad.
jokes.explanation: 'A van with a car engine' is a wonderful specific detail that raises more questions than it answers (is a car engine in a van unusual? Is this a downgrade?). The distinction is meaningless but Criss delivers it with complete conviction, revealing his pride in a fundamentally embarrassing enterprise. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: NBC just becomes a web site that sells used office supplies.
jokes.setup: Criss imagines worst-case scenarios where Liz loses her job.
jokes.punchline: NBC becoming a website that sells used office supplies — a meta joke about NBC's decline that also references the show's history (NBC's corporate dysfunction is a recurring 30 Rock theme).
jokes.explanation: Good 30 Rock meta-joke — NBC's real-world struggles with relevance make 'used office supplies website' a pointed but not mean-spirited dig. Rewatch bonus for fans who appreciate the show's NBC satire throughline.

jokes.text: Of course, because you're the person who has to krang that plant for nine months, poop it, and then go back to work to support both of you!
jokes.setup: Liz asks why the baby conversation stresses Criss out.
jokes.punchline: 'Krang that plant for nine months, poop it' — Criss adopts the 'plant' euphemism (from earlier) but uses the invented word 'krang' for gestation, and 'poop it' for birth. The made-up word is the highlight.
jokes.explanation: 'Krang' is a brilliant invented word — slightly aggressive-sounding, vaguely biological, perfect as a verb for pregnancy. 'Poop it' for giving birth is crude but the word choice within the plant metaphor is consistent and funny. A strong callback that escalates the original plant metaphor. Justifies 8.0.

jokes.text: Somebody with money that's probably named Spencer or Grant. And he has a watch, and an office with a trash can and a little basketball hoop on it. And he plays as hard as he works because, damn it, he deserves to blow off a little steam.
jokes.setup: Criss accuses Liz of wanting a wealthy conventional partner instead of him.
jokes.punchline: The character of 'Spencer or Grant' is built in real time with escalating specificity — the office basketball hoop, the work-life philosophy — until Criss has constructed a complete imaginary rival with satiric precision.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character escalation — Criss builds the imaginary 'Grant' with mounting specificity (the basket hoop on the trash can, 'plays as hard as he works') until it becomes a perfect satirical portrait of a certain type of finance-bro. 'Damn it, he deserves to blow off a little steam' is the perfect kicker.

jokes.text: God, I don't wanna be with Spencer! / And yet you're silent about Grant.
jokes.setup: Liz protests that she doesn't want the hypothetical wealthy man.
jokes.punchline: Criss notes she only denied Spencer, not Grant — implying a specific attraction to the Grant archetype.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback structure with maximum economy. 'And yet you're silent about Grant' is nine words that perfectly skewer Liz and pay off the preceding bit. The specificity of tracking which name she denied is precise comedy writing.

jokes.text: Well, guess what... I'm gonna become Grant. That's right, tomorrow I'm gonna take my truck out, and I'm gonna start pulling my weight, like a man. Now, get in that bed, and let's watch Dance Moms.
jokes.setup: Criss declares he'll become the responsible provider Grant represents.
jokes.punchline: He undercuts his masculine declaration immediately by demanding they watch Dance Moms — the most emasculating possible television choice.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from masculine declaration ('pulling my weight, like a man') to 'let's watch Dance Moms' in the same breath is well-timed. Character-specific to Criss's contradictions.

jokes.text: Are you crying because there are no roles for actresses in their 40s, nor should there be?
jokes.setup: Tracy finds Jenna crying in the hallway.
jokes.punchline: 'Nor should there be' — Tracy casually endorses Hollywood ageism against women with complete sincerity, the second half of the sentence doing all the damage.
jokes.explanation: 'Nor should there be' is the essential addition — without it, it's just an observation. With it, it becomes a perfect Tracy Jordan moment: he identifies the problem and immediately affirms it as correct. The economy is exceptional (the entire payload is in five words). Justifies 8.3.

jokes.text: I once did 100 takes and still couldn't say the word 'incorrigible.' Great, now I get it!
jokes.setup: Jenna says she did 50 takes and couldn't do it; Tracy commiserates with his own story.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's story: 100 takes on 'incorrigible' — and he understands the word only NOW, in this conversation. The delivery implies he's heard it somewhere just now and finally cracked it.
jokes.explanation: A classic Tracy Jordan beat — he's only tangentially following the conversation, and when he suddenly 'gets' a word at a delayed moment, it's perfectly in character. 'Great, now I get it!' is a lovely throwaway revelation.

jokes.text: I have someone inside me too. It's a bath toy of a scuba diver.
jokes.setup: Jenna says she has her old self 'inside her, taking over.'
jokes.punchline: Tracy responds to the metaphor literally — he also has something inside him, specifically a bath toy scuba diver.
jokes.explanation: Pure Tracy Jordan genius. He takes a metaphorical statement and responds with a medically alarming literal one. 'A bath toy of a scuba diver' is specific enough to suggest it's true, which makes it funnier and darker. The economy is perfect — one sentence raises infinite questions. Justifies 8.2.

jokes.text: Jessica Tandy's zombie is coming to find you. Is that correct? / Yes, siri. Thank you, baby.
jokes.setup: Tracy tries to interpret Jenna's freak-out for Siri.
jokes.punchline: He summarizes her crisis as 'Jessica Tandy's zombie is coming to find you' and then thanks Siri as 'baby' — a complete misreading and a weirdly intimate relationship with his phone.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's relationship with Siri is always funny in context — 'Thank you, baby' implies he's genuinely affectionate with the AI. The zombie misinterpretation is a good escalation of the Siri bit.

jokes.text: So, Lemon, I took your advice and used my transgression with Diana as a weapon to interrogate Avery, just as you suggested. / That is not what I suggested. / You just hear what you want to hear. / Thank you. They're from Italy.
jokes.setup: Jack claims Liz suggested his manipulation scheme.
jokes.punchline: When Liz says 'you just hear what you want to hear,' Jack mishears it as a compliment about his ears ('Thank you. They're from Italy.') — perfectly demonstrating the very thing she's accusing him of.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structural joke — Jack proves Liz's accusation ('you just hear what you want to hear') by immediately mishearing it. The meta-circularity is perfect. 'They're from Italy' implies he thinks she's complimenting his ears' appearance/origin. The structure mirrors the content: he hears a compliment about himself where there isn't one. This is one of the two best jokes in the episode, justifying 8.7/9.0. Comparable to top-tier 30 Rock writing.

jokes.text: Drop a grenade in that bunker, like Jim Brown in The Dirty Dozen. Enjoy your party, Nazis!
jokes.setup: Jack describes his plan to force Avery out of her 'forgiveness bunker.'
jokes.punchline: He extends the military metaphor into a specific Dirty Dozen movie reference, complete with an in-character line for Jim Brown — 'Enjoy your party, Nazis!' — as if quoting the film.
jokes.explanation: A fun Jack character beat — his tendency to use military/film metaphors for domestic situations is well-established. 'Enjoy your party, Nazis!' is a good absurdist film quote invention. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: God, she's good. This kind of gamesmanship is why I love her. She has the brain of a man, and the ass of a French teenager.
jokes.setup: Jack realizes Avery is better at the mind games than he expected.
jokes.punchline: His compliment: 'the brain of a man, and the ass of a French teenager' — the sexism of the 'brain of a man' combined with the specific and slightly disturbing 'ass of a French teenager' makes this a classic Jack Donaghy excess.
jokes.explanation: Peak Jack Donaghy compliment — the formula of 'the [X] of a [person], and the [Y] of a [other person]' is his signature. 'The ass of a French teenager' is gratuitously specific in the way only Jack's compliments are. High character integration.

jokes.text: I do, Lemon. I wear the pants. / Nice pants, Avery. / And, Liz, good to see you. Your hair's the same. / It's not. Actually, something terrible happened.
jokes.setup: Jack insists he wears the pants in his marriage; Avery enters, admires Jack's pants, and dismisses Liz.
jokes.punchline: The visual/tonal payoff: Avery enters and immediately reestablishes dominance (complimenting Jack's literal pants, dismissing Liz's hair) — proving Jack's claim wrong through demonstration. And Liz's 'something terrible happened' to her hair plays as a dark offhand callback.
jokes.explanation: Elegant multi-layer joke: (1) Jack's claim of dominance is undermined by Avery's entrance, (2) Avery admires his literal pants (making the 'wear the pants' metaphor literal), (3) Liz's hair devastation is played as a tragic aside. The scene compression is excellent 30 Rock structure.

jokes.text: Lloyd Blankfein slithers back into the sewers to eat rotten fish at 6:00.
jokes.setup: Avery mentions she has a finance presentation with Lloyd Blankfein (Goldman Sachs CEO).
jokes.punchline: She describes him as literally sewer-dwelling and fish-eating — dehumanizing the Goldman Sachs CEO as a creature.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'rotten fish' and 'slithers back into the sewers' makes this more than a generic banker joke — it's a precise dehumanization with good imagery. Very Avery's worldview (she accepts this as normal).

jokes.text: [Rapping] ♪ Deathly Hallows and Tebow / Oprah does her last show / Beyoncé had a baby, yo / It's a 12-month wrap-up, rap-rap-rap-up ♪
jokes.setup: Liz presents her one-hour pop culture catch-up for Avery in rap form.
jokes.punchline: The entire year of culture condensed into a four-line rap with 'rap-rap-rap-up' as both conclusion and the worst possible rhyme — Liz's earnest effort at multimedia presentation.
jokes.explanation: The joke is both the absurdity of a rap presentation and the specific cultural touchstones chosen (Tebow, Oprah finale, royal baby). 'Rap-rap-rap-up' is a delightfully bad pun that fits Liz's earnest effort perfectly.

jokes.text: You know what, I'll just read some US Weeklies. / Thank you, Lemon. / But it's an hour long, like you wanted. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Liz's rap presentation is rejected immediately; Jack cuts her off.
jokes.punchline: Jack's 'Thank you, Lemon' after the rap is a masterpiece of polite dismissal; Liz's protest that it's an hour long gets the same 'Thank you' — the repetition confirming that he's done.
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'Thank you, Lemon' / 'Thank you' is good sitcom rhythm — the second one lands harder because it's the same dismissal for a different protest. Functional but not outstanding.

jokes.text: And no matter what you say, I am always going to forgive you. Always.
jokes.setup: Jack keeps escalating his confessions trying to break Avery's forgiveness shield.
jokes.punchline: Avery's absolute, steely commitment to forgiveness as a weapon — 'always' delivered with quiet menace — is funnier than any reaction would be.
jokes.explanation: The joke is the weaponization of a virtue — Avery's forgiveness has become more threatening than anger would be. The scene plays as a thriller beat that's also a comedy beat. The understatement is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: It's a brand new location, Liz. I got a subway entrance right here, and I got a tour bus stop right there. Also, FOX News is right across the street, and word is Greta Van Susteren eats hot dogs like Slimer.
jokes.setup: Criss has found a new location for his hot dog truck.
jokes.punchline: The biggest selling point: Greta Van Susteren (Fox News host) 'eats hot dogs like Slimer' — comparing a real TV personality to the Ghostbusters ghost is both random and oddly specific.
jokes.explanation: 'Eats hot dogs like Slimer' is a very specific, slightly mean celebrity comparison that's funny because of its randomness and the vivid image of voracious hot dog consumption. Slimer eating hot dogs is an excellent visual reference.

jokes.text: Right, those creepy, off-brand Sesame Street characters that harass tourists into paying them to take pictures. I hate those guys. As a Sesame Street purist, I don't think Elmo usually tells passing women they have a sweet dumper.
jokes.setup: Criss has set up at a spot occupied by Sesame Street costumed characters.
jokes.punchline: Liz declares herself a 'Sesame Street purist' and notes that the real Elmo doesn't typically compliment women's backsides ('sweet dumper') — treating Times Square street performers as heretics against canon.
jokes.explanation: 'Sesame Street purist' is a great Liz Lemon character detail — she takes children's television seriously. 'Sweet dumper' as Elmo's unwanted commentary is a crude but well-executed detail. The combination is very Liz.

jokes.text: Legally, I have to say I'm Elmarg!
jokes.setup: Criss fights the fake Elmo performer for the corner.
jokes.punchline: In mid-fight, the performer stops to clarify his legal non-trademark name — 'Elmarg' — continuing the fiction that he's not infringing on the real Elmo IP even while brawling.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant detail — the legal disclaimer ('Legally, I have to say...') during a street fight is perfectly absurd. 'Elmarg' is an inspired fake name (just adding a 'g'). The incongruity of IP law compliance during violence is peak 30 Rock absurdism. Highly quotable. Justifies 8.0.

jokes.text: Them puppets done picked the wrong day to cross my kin! It's on, panhandle style!
jokes.setup: Jenna arrives to find Criss in a fight with the Sesame Street characters.
jokes.punchline: Jenna immediately goes full 'Jay-nuh' — Southern dialect, kinship language ('my kin'), and 'panhandle style' as a fighting descriptor — revealing she's completely lost control of her inner dirtbag.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character payoff — Jenna's inner Southern girl emerges at the worst possible moment for her 'classy' image, and the specific dialect ('done picked,' 'my kin,' 'panhandle style') is well-calibrated. 'Panhandle style' is a wonderfully specific invented fighting style. High character integration.

jokes.text: Well, it's over. I'm never gonna get a wedding sponsor now. That dirtbag Jay-nuh won. I wanted my wedding to be an expression of who I am, and now it will be. I'm a panhandle hick, and my wedding will be just another panel on my mother's family history back tattoo.
jokes.setup: After the fight, Jenna despairs about her image.
jokes.punchline: 'My wedding will be just another panel on my mother's family history back tattoo' — the back tattoo as a family chronicle is a perfectly specific detail of low-income Southern culture.
jokes.explanation: The 'family history back tattoo' is an inspired detail — it implies an entire family tradition of commemorating life events through tattoo panels on one person's back. Specific, original, and very funny as a class signifier.

jokes.text: So you own things. That's good. 'Christian...' That's always a good word. Wait, did they say 'Christian' about my shoes? 'With her Christian Louboutins.' They didn't know that my shoes were cheap knockoffs. They thought they were fancy, even though they're secretly crap.
jokes.setup: Liz tries to cheer Jenna up by pointing out the photo caption mentions she 'owns things.'
jokes.punchline: Jenna realizes the paparazzi misidentified her knockoffs as real Louboutins — giving her the upscale image she couldn't earn through acting.
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff — the knockoff shoes from earlier now solve Jenna's identity crisis. The beat-by-beat revelation (reading the caption piece by piece) is well-structured. Functions more as plot than pure joke but has genuine comedic payoff.

jokes.text: That's it. That's who I am! I'm that knockoff designer shoe. My outside is shiny and pretty, but my inside is filled with cardboard and horse glue.
jokes.setup: Jenna has an epiphany about her identity based on the shoes.
jokes.punchline: 'My inside is filled with cardboard and horse glue' — Jenna extends the knockoff shoe metaphor to her own interior, suggesting her entire personality is cheap filler material.
jokes.explanation: The metaphor extended to its logical conclusion is excellent — 'cardboard and horse glue' is specific enough to be genuinely funny rather than just a vague 'empty inside' statement. Jenna accepting this as her identity is perfectly in character. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: No, I think it's a very cool costume, mayor Bloomberg. Tonight, I'm mayor Booo-mberg. Yes, I think you've mentioned that. Booo... booo...
jokes.setup: Jack interacts with Mayor Bloomberg at the party.
jokes.punchline: Bloomberg is apparently in a ghost costume ('Booo-mberg') and keeps insisting on his party identity while Jack politely tolerates it. The mayor of New York reduced to repeating 'booo' at a party.
jokes.explanation: 'Mayor Booo-mberg' is a pun that earns its keep because it's deployed so casually — and the repeated 'Booo...' implies Bloomberg is committed to the bit in a way that's more funny than dignified. The celebrity cameo-as-joke works.

jokes.text: How about this? A few months ago, Liddy broke into the gun safe and shot up your gift-wrapping room. / I did wear your nightgowns. Not to feel you near, they're just comfortable. / I had an erotic dream about an adult Dora the Explorer.
jokes.setup: Jack, desperate to get Avery to confess, starts revealing increasingly damaging truths.
jokes.punchline: A three-part escalation: (1) Liddy shot up the gift-wrapping room, (2) He wore Avery's nightgowns (not sentimental, just comfortable), (3) He had an erotic dream about adult Dora the Explorer — each revelation more damaging than the last.
jokes.explanation: This three-confession sequence is exceptional 30 Rock writing. The escalation structure is flawless: guns/child danger → cross-dressing with non-sentimental explanation → erotic children's cartoon dream. Each beat is funnier than the last. The nightgown callback (Avery mentioned them being stretched out) is perfectly planted. 'Adult Dora the Explorer' is a brilliantly specific and disturbing erotic fixation. The 'not to feel you near, they're just comfortable' dismissal of the sentimental excuse is a masterwork of Jack Donaghy pride. Justifies 8.7/9.0. Comparable to the Snip-snap anchor example in escalation structure.

jokes.text: I took her on a balcony in Madrid, above the Plaza Mayor. She had flowers in her hair.
jokes.setup: Jack describes his erotic Dora the Explorer dream.
jokes.punchline: The dream is elaborately specific and romantic — balcony, Madrid, Plaza Mayor, flowers in her hair — treating a children's cartoon character with the reverence of a real romantic encounter.
jokes.explanation: The continuation of the Dora dream joke is MORE disturbing and MORE funny because of its specificity. Jack doesn't just mention the dream — he's clearly thought about it. 'She had flowers in her hair' is the perfect romantic detail that makes it transcendently absurd. Justifies 8.2.

jokes.text: Until the flight home, the only words I'd ever said to Scott Scottsman were, 'and now with sports, Scott Scottsman.'
jokes.setup: Avery reveals she never had a relationship with Scott — the apparent red flag was nothing.
jokes.punchline: Their only interaction was her scripted anchor handoff — 'and now with sports, Scott Scottsman' — a perfectly deflating reveal that their entire 'relationship' was professional formality.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback with perfect economy. The entire mystery of Scott Scottsman is deflated by revealing their whole relationship was a scripted anchor handoff — 'and now with sports, Scott Scottsman' — which we heard in the opening. The repetition of the exact phrase pays off the North Korean broadcast sequences.

jokes.text: We need a new blender anyway.
jokes.setup: Jack says 'that's what we're gonna do. We're gonna renew our vows!'
jokes.punchline: Avery's non-sequitur: 'We need a new blender anyway' — implying that vow renewal is, practically speaking, just an opportunity to register for gifts again.
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan — five words that completely undercut a romantic moment by making it purely transactional. Avery reduces vow renewal to appliance acquisition, which is both darkly funny and perfectly in character for a practical, unsentimental Avery Jessup. Maximum economy. Highly quotable. Justifies 8.2.

jokes.text: Criss got into a fight with an Elmo. And he hates it that I make more money than he does. And I don't know, maybe we're not supposed to have a plant together.
jokes.setup: Liz arrives late at the party and explains why.
jokes.punchline: She lists three things as if they're equivalent: Elmo fight, financial resentment, and existential doubt about having a baby (still called 'a plant') — the plant callback recontextualizing the other two as equal-level concerns.
jokes.explanation: Functional callback that ties up the Liz/Criss subplot. The list structure works and 'plant' maintains the established vocabulary. More plot recap than pure comedy but still carries the episode's tone.

jokes.text: No, no, renewing vows is a kiss of death. You should have let me finish my rap. There was a whole verse about it! ♪ J-Lo and Marc Anthony / Donny and Vicki from O.C. / 12-month wrap-up, rap-rap-rap-up ♪ It's the kiss of death, yo! I reject Chris Brown's comeback! Lemon out!
jokes.setup: Jack and Avery announce vow renewal; Liz objects.
jokes.punchline: Liz delivers more of her rap (citing J-Lo/Marc Anthony and Donny/Vicki as vow renewal cautionary tales), then dramatically exits with 'I reject Chris Brown's comeback! Lemon out!' — a non-sequitur sign-off that names a controversial celebrity.
jokes.explanation: A strong episode closer for the Liz subplot — the rap callback, the vow renewal warning with specific celebrity examples, and 'Lemon out!' as a signature exit. 'I reject Chris Brown's comeback' is a topically dark non-sequitur that works as an absurd exclamation point. The 'rap-rap-rap-up' callback is satisfying.

jokes.text: I reject Chris Brown's comeback! Lemon out!
jokes.setup: Liz is making her dramatic exit from the party.
jokes.punchline: Her mic-drop line is a non-sequitur cultural position statement — rejecting Chris Brown's comeback as if it's related to anything that just happened — delivered as a closing declaration.
jokes.explanation: 'Lemon out!' as a mic-drop closer is very Liz — she's been doing 'dramatic exit' gags throughout the series. 'I reject Chris Brown's comeback' as the content of the exit statement is perfect: it's topical, opinionated, and completely disconnected from the conversation she just had. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Here at off-brandheelz.com, we've got all the brands that fit your needs and your budget. Johnny Choon, Dolce and Banana, Merolo Blornig, Prader, Gukki, DKNI, Alexandorp McKing, Diana Von Fistenbug, and Jessica Simpson.
jokes.setup: A fake commercial for a knockoff shoe website — the episode's tag.
jokes.punchline: A list of mangled designer names: Jimmy Choo → Johnny Choon, Dolce & Gabbana → Dolce and Banana, Manolo Blahnik → Merolo Blornig, Prada → Prader, Gucci → Gukki, DKNY → DKNI, Alexander McQueen → Alexandorp McKing, Diane Von Furstenberg → Diana Von Fistenbug — and then 'Jessica Simpson' (real, no alteration needed).
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sequences — each name is its own micro-joke, with varying degrees of corruption of the original brand. The cumulative effect is excellent. The kicker 'Jessica Simpson' (left unaltered) is the perfect punchline: she IS the off-brand designer. 'Diana Von Fistenbug' and 'Dolce and Banana' are the strongest individual entries. Justifies 8.3/9.0.

jokes.text: Job interviews, running from your parole officer, attending a theater opening, breaking into your mom's house to steal her cable box.
jokes.setup: The fake commercial lists use cases for the shoes.
jokes.punchline: Starting with legitimate occasions (job interviews, theater) and escalating to criminal activities (evading parole officers, burglarizing mom's cable box) — the escalation reveals the intended market.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke — the commercial format sets up legitimate uses and then reveals the actual target market through increasingly illegal activities. 'Breaking into your mom's house to steal her cable box' is the perfect endpoint: crime, but petty and domestic. Very 30 Rock in its specific absurdism.

jokes.text: off-brandheelz.com, naturally fayun-cy.
jokes.setup: The commercial's sign-off tagline.
jokes.punchline: 'Naturally fayun-cy' — a deliberately misspelled/mispronounced 'naturally fancy' that sounds like both a dialect pronunciation and a brand affectation, perfectly encapsulating the knockoff aesthetic.
jokes.explanation: 'Fayun-cy' is a perfect pronunciation joke — it sounds like a discount-store accent trying to sound upscale and failing. Maximum economy for a tagline. Good punctuation mark for the commercial sequence.

tmdb_overview: Avery finally returns home from her kidnapping ordeal in North Korea, yet Jack grows uncertain of her fidelity while she was away. Elsewhere, Criss is crossed due to Liz's role as top wage earner, and Jenna seeks a sponsor for her approaching nuptials.
insight: Avery's return fuels 69 jokes in 42 minutes, hitting escalation peaks mid-episode.
